yudha2021.researcherid-numbers: Tjahjono, Benny/X-3269-2019 Longhurst, Phil/A-2454-2010 Tjahjono, Benny/D-5077-2009
yudha2021.abstract: The study described in this paper uses direct evidence from processes applied for the developing economy of Indonesia, as it defines the trajectory for its future energy policy and energy research agenda. The paper addresses the research gap to make explicit the process undertaken by key stakeholders in assessing and determining the suitability, feasibility, and dynamics of the renewable energy sector. Barriers and enablers that are key in selecting the most suitable renewable energy sources for developing economies for the renewable energy development have been identified from extensive analyses of research documents alongside qualitative data from the Focus Group Discussions (FGD). The selected FGD participants encompass the collective views that cut across the political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental aspects of renewable energy development in Indonesia. The information gained from the FGD gives insights into the outlook and challenges that are central to energy transition within the country, alongside the perceptions of renewable energy development from the influential stakeholders contributing to the process. It is notable that the biggest barriers to transition are centred on planning and implementation aspects, as it is also evident that many in the community do not adhere to the same vision.
yudha2021.title: Stakeholders' Recount on the Dynamics of Indonesia's Renewable Energy Sector
yudha2021.author: Yudha, Satya Widya and Tjahjono, Benny and Longhurst, Philip
yudha2021.description: Examines stakeholder processes for assessing renewable energy suitability in Indonesia, identifying barriers and enablers through focus group discussions across political, economic, social, technological, legal, and environmental dimensions.

yusuf2024.abstract: The energy transition toward Net Zero Emission by 2060 hinges on the renewable energy power plants in Indonesia. Good practices in several countries suggest a peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading system using blockchain technology, supported by renewable energy (solar panels), an innovation to provide equal access to sustainable electricity while reducing the impact of climate change. The P2P energy trading concept has a higher social potential than the conventional electricity buying and selling approach, such as that of PLN (the state-owned electricity company in Indonesia), which applies the network management concept but does not have a sharing element. This model implements a solar-powered mini-grid system and produces a smart contract that facilitates electricity network users to buy, sell, and trade electricity in rural areas via smartphones. This study aims to measure the stakeholders' perceptions of the peer-to-peer (P2P) energy trading model using blockchain technology in the Gumelar District, Banyumas Regency, Central Java Province, Indonesia. The stakeholders in question are representatives of Households (producers and consumers), Government, State Electricity Company (PLN), Non-Governmental Organizations, Private Sector and Academician. Measurement of perception in this study used a questionnaire approach with a Likert scale. The results of filling out the questionnaire were analyzed using four methods: IFE/EFE matrix; IE matrix; SWOT matrix; and SPACE matrix to assess the results and their suitability to each other. The results of the stakeholder perception assessment show that there are 44 internal factors and 33 external factors that can influence this model. We obtained an IFE and EFE score of 2.92 and 2.83 for the internal and external results using the IE matrix. These place the model in quadrant V, meaning the P2P model can survive in the long term to generate profits. Based on the SWOT analysis results, this model is located at the coordinate point -0.40, 0.31, placing it in quadrant II. This means that the P2P model is in a competitive situation and faces threats but still has internal strengths. Based on the SPACE matrix, stakeholder perception states that the P2P model is at coordinate point 1, -0.3. This shows that the P2P model has the potential to be a competitive advantage in its type of activity that continues to grow. In conclusion, our findings show that stakeholders' perceptions of P2P models using blockchain technology can be implemented effectively and provide social, economic, and environmental incentives.
yusuf2024.title: Stakeholders' Perceptions of the Peer-to-Peer Energy Trading Model Using Blockchain Technology in Indonesia
yusuf2024.author: Yusuf, Faisal and Sari, Riri Fitri and Yusgiantoro, Purnomo and Soesilo, Tri Edhi Budhi
yusuf2024.description: Stakeholder perception assessment of peer-to-peer blockchain-based energy trading model implementation in rural Indonesia using strategic analysis matrices.
yusuf2024.method: Survey with Likert scale questionnaire, analyzed using IFE/EFE, IE, SWOT, and SPACE matrices

zaheb2024.abstract: The growing global concern for climate change and the need for sustainable energy solutions have driven nations to explore renewable energy alternatives. This research focuses on a developing country heavily reliant on imported electricity and evaluates the potential of renewable energy resources. Using the Analytical Hierarchy Process (AHP), a multi-criteria decision-making method (MCDM), this study prioritizes sustainable energy resources crucial for energy security and environmental sustainability, given the country's dependence on traditional and imported power and its potential for renewable energy development. This study employs AHP to evaluate and rank various sustainable energy options, emphasizing their technological, economic, environmental, and social impacts. The novelty of this research lies in its comprehensive and systematic approach to integrating diverse expert opinions and utilizing AHP; the development of a robust decision-making model that accommodates the diverse criteria and sub-criteria (SCs) influencing the prioritization of energy resources; and its bridging of the gaps through the integration of varied criteria and SCs, region-specific concerns, and stakeholders' engagement by creating a comprehensive and inclusive prioritization strategy. The key findings highlight solar energy as the most viable sustainable energy resource, followed by wind and hydro energy. These results underscore the significant potential for solar energy development, considering its current technological advancements, economic affordability, social acceptance, and environmental friendliness. This study not only provides a prioritized list of sustainable energy resources but also offers a methodological framework adaptable for similar assessments in other regions facing energy transition challenges. Readers will find a detailed explanation of the AHP methodology, the criteria used for evaluating energy resources, and the implications of the findings for policy and decision making. This research is particularly relevant for policymakers, energy planners, and stakeholders interested in sustainable energy development and strategic planning in similar contexts.
zaheb2024.title: Comprehensive Analysis and Prioritization of Sustainable Energy Resources Using Analytical Hierarchy Process
zaheb2024.author: Zaheb, Hameedullah and Obaidi, Obaidullah and Mukhtar, Sarban and Shirani, Habiburahman and Ahmadi, Mikaeel and Yona, Atsushi
zaheb2024.description: Multi-criteria decision-making analysis prioritizing sustainable energy resources using AHP methodology in a developing country context

zaman2018.researcherid-numbers: Islam, Nazrul/AAO-9069-2020 Brudermann, Thomas/ABH-3138-2020 Kumar, S./K-2977-2014
zaman2018.abstract: Socio-technical transformations towards low-carbon energy systems are on the way in developed countries. Conversely, developing countries tend to be locked in fossil fuels and foster coal-based energy structures, emphasizing reliable and cost-effective energy provision and sidelining environmental concerns. In this study, we identified and analysed the predominant factors related to coal-based power generation in Bangladesh. We applied a mixed-method approach, initially conducting a systematic literature review and, subsequently, semi structured expert interviews to identify and validate relevant factors. We then assessed their relative importance using an Analytical Hierarchy Process based on expert judgments. The results of this assessment reveal that socio-economic aspects and environmental issues scored highest, while technological aspects and sector regulations were considered to be less relevant for large-scale coal power implementation. We conclude that future energy policies created in Bangladesh will need to use appropriate legal instruments and address issues such as human displacement and resettlement, low levels of public acceptance, health hazards and environmental pollution. Participative policy frameworks should be deployed in coal plant projects, and active monitoring systems are necessary to reduce the negative consequences associated with increased electrification and energy consumption. To address foreseeable structural challenges, it furthermore will be crucial to explore sustainable alternatives.
zaman2018.title: A Multi-Criteria Analysis of Coal-Based Power Generation in Bangladesh
zaman2018.author: Zaman, Rafia and Brudermann, Thomas and Kumar, S. and Islam, Nazrul
zaman2018.description: Analyzes factors influencing coal-based power generation in Bangladesh using mixed methods and Analytical Hierarchy Process to assess relative importance of socio-economic, environmental, technological, and regulatory dimensions.
zaman2018.method: Mixed-method (systematic literature review, semi-structured expert interviews, Analytical Hierarchy Process)

zaunbrecher2018.abstract: To foster a socially accepted energy transition, it is essential to gain insights into motives for acceptance or rejection of technologies related to renewable energies. The study aims to shed light on the emotional evaluation of renewable energy technologies and in how far the affective responses are correlated with the acceptance of those technologies. An empirical study is conducted in which a semantic differential is used to assess emotional evaluation of wind power, solar power (PV) and biomass for electricity production. Furthermore, general acceptance of the technologies was assessed. It was found that not only did the technologies differ in terms of emotional responses they evoked, but that those responses also varied significantly between groups of high and low levels of acceptance concerning the respective energy technology. By analyzing spontaneous associations with the three energy sources, possible reasons for the affective evaluations were identified, which can provide essential topics for the communication about those technologies. Overall, the three renewable energy technologies revealed different emotional evaluations which might considerably impact the overall acceptance. It is argued that knowledge about such affective perceptions is useful to tailor energy technology development in early phases and to steer public information and communication strategies.
zaunbrecher2018.editor: Klein, C and Donnellan, B and Helfert, M
zaunbrecher2018.title: The Good, the Bad and the Ugly: Affect and Its Role for Renewable Energy Acceptance
zaunbrecher2018.booktitle: Proceedings of the 7th International Conference on Smart Cities and Green Ict Systems (Smartgreens)
zaunbrecher2018.author: Zaunbrecher, Barbara S. and Arning, Katrin and Ziefle, Martina
zaunbrecher2018.description: Examines how emotional evaluation of renewable energy technologies (wind, solar, biomass) correlates with acceptance levels and identifies communication strategies.
zaunbrecher2018.method: Survey with semantic differential for emotional evaluation and acceptance assessment

zaunbrecher2019.abstract: The sustainable energy transition (Energiewende) is a multidisciplinary challenge. While for technical disciplines, the focus is on the development of technologies which can supply, transmit and store energy in a sustainable way, economic research focuses for example on the analyses of costs and risks of different asset portfolios. Yet another perspective is taken by the social sciences who focus on social challenges associated with the implementation of measures for realizing the Energiewende (decarbonization, high energy efficiency, high shares of renewables, nuclear phaseout), for example their acceptability. A solution for energy supply and storage which is optimized only according to one of these perspectives will, however, fail to meet other essential criteria. To develop sustainable solutions for energy supply and storage, which are technically feasible, cost-effective, and supported by local residents, interdisciplinary cooperation of researchers is thus needed. Interdisciplinary research, however, is subject to many barriers, for example the need to agree on a common analytical framework. In this paper, a process model for interdisciplinary energy research is proposed, in which specific scenarios are used to aid interdisciplinary cooperation and reciprocal integration of results. Based on a current research project, the phases of the model and the use of the scenarios in disciplinary and interdisciplinary work packages are described, as well as challenges and shortcomings of the model.
zaunbrecher2019.series: Communications in Computer and Information Science
zaunbrecher2019.editor: Donnellan, B and Klein, C and Helfert, M and Gusikhin, O and Pascoal, A
zaunbrecher2019.title: Using Energy Supply Scenarios in an Interdisciplinary Research Process
zaunbrecher2019.booktitle: Smart Cities, Green Technologies, and Intelligent Transport Systems, Smartgreens 2017
zaunbrecher2019.author: Zaunbrecher, Barbara S. and Bexten, Thomas and Specht, Jan Martin and Wirsum, Manfred and Madlener, Reinhard and Ziefle, Martina
zaunbrecher2019.description: Proposes interdisciplinary process model using scenarios to integrate technical, economic, and social perspectives in energy transition research.
zaunbrecher2019.method: Process model development based on current research project

zeyringer2016.abstract: Low-carbon technologies need to be commercially available soon to play a relevant part in the energy transition. The UK has excellent potential for wind and wave power. The costs of wind energy are cost-competitive but there are issues with intermittency and public acceptance of onshore wind. Marine energy could provide a more stable electricity source but has significant uncertainty about future costs and deployment risks. What role do ocean and wind energy play in a cost effective, technically feasible long-term low carbon energy system? We study the necessary technological learning of tidal energy with UKTM (a long running energy system model) and analyse the impacts of adding tidal to the electricity system with highRES (a high spatial and temporal resolution electricity system model). We find that while tidal energy reduces the need for investment into flexible generation, it does so less than the spatial diversification of already existing renewable energy sources. Translating the results into policy advice it may be time to pick existing technologies (in this case wind energy) as winners.
zeyringer2016.series: International Conference on the European Energy Market
zeyringer2016.publisher: INESC TEC; IEEE Power & Energy Soc; IEEE
zeyringer2016.title: ``New'' or ``Old'' Technologies to Decarbonize UK's Electricity System? A Long-Term High Spatial and Temporal Resolution Assessment for Marine and Wind Energy
zeyringer2016.booktitle: 2016 13th International Conference on the European Energy Market (Eem)
zeyringer2016.author: Zeyringer, Marianne and Fais, Birgit and Price, James
zeyringer2016.description: Compares tidal and wind energy roles in UK's cost-effective low-carbon electricity system using energy system modeling.
zeyringer2016.epistemic_model: Energy system modeling and techno-economic optimization
zeyringer2016.method: Energy system modeling (UKTM and highRES models)

zhang2022.abstract: The EU and China are both pioneers in energy transition and are major energy consumers. However, we know little about the attitude of the Chinese public toward EU's energy role or EU-China energy cooperation. The paper contributes to the study of relationship between agenda-setting and public opinion in the context of Chinese social media. Using empirical data, it finds that energy cooperation, energy trading, energy politics, and energy technology&service are the four co-occurrence networks of Chinese public discussion on the topic. Yet the opinion leaders differ on these issues. While verified media accounts are key opinion leaders setting the agenda in EU energy politics and trade issues, in energy technology and service issues, verified individual accounts lead opinions. The study helps understand the role of online opinion leaders in EU-China energy relations and argues that key opinion leaders need to play more active roles in communicating the issues and guiding public discussions.
zhang2022.title: Public Attitude and Opinion Leaders: Mapping Chinese Discussion of Eu's Energy Role on Social Media
zhang2022.author: Zhang, Li and Wang, Peinan
zhang2022.description: Examines Chinese public opinion on EU-China energy cooperation through social media analysis, revealing how different opinion leader types shape discourse across energy domains.
zhang2022.epistemic_model: Agenda-setting theory, public opinion formation, social media communication
zhang2022.method: Empirical data analysis of Chinese social media co-occurrence networks

zimm2019.abstract: Historically, long-waves have characterized transformations of the energy systems. There is not much reason to assume that our current energy system is here to stay. One possible future option is that renewables will provide all energy needed. While many scenarios exist showing that this is technically feasible, the related costs, speed of technology diffusion and social and political acceptance of such an energy transition are fiercely debated, both in the scientific field as well as in politics. Yet, there is growing consensus that renewables are becoming established as a key building block in the energy system, irrespective of the exact shares they represent. The focus should shift from a debate surrounding the feasibility of a 100% renewable system to how we can enable a speedy and immediate upscaling.
zimm2019.title: Is the Renewables Transformation a Piece of Cake or a Pie in the Sky?
zimm2019.author: Zimm, Caroline and Goldemberg, Jose and Nakicenovic, Nebojsa and Busch, Sebastian
zimm2019.description: Examines the shift from debating technical feasibility of 100% renewable energy systems to enabling rapid upscaling and deployment.
zimm2019.epistemic_model: Energy transition theory, socio-technical systems analysis

zuk2023.abstract: The aim of this article is to analyse the relationship between the sense of social security and the anticipated socio-economic deprivation of the Turoszow Basin's residents in Poland related to the decarbonisation process, and their attitudes to energy transition and climate challenges. Article draws attention to the close relationship between the perception of economic challenges and of threats to social security and attitudes towards climate and environmental issues among the residents of coal basins. These multidimensional factors shaping opinions on energy transition ultimately translate into ideological and political sympathies. Based on the results of surveys carried out on a sample of 1000 people living in the region, the author defends the thesis that energy transition cannot be treated only as a process of technological change or a bundle of single regional economic transformations resulting from decarbonisation, particularly in regions dependent on the mining industry. The obtained results indicate that not only does the current economic and financial situation of coal basin residents shape their attitudes to the decarbonisation process, but also their anticipated personal material situation after the closure of the mine and the implementation of energy transition may have a great impact on the current assessment of transition goals as well as their perception of climate change and the negative effects of the mining industry.
zuk2023.title: The Sense of Socio-Economic Threat and the Perception of Climate Challenges and Attitudes towards Energy Transition among Residents of Coal Basins: The Case of Turoszow Basin in Poland
zuk2023.author: Zuk, Piotr
zuk2023.description: Analyzes how anticipated socio-economic deprivation and social security concerns shape coal basin residents' attitudes toward energy transition and climate challenges in Poland's Turoszow Basin.
zuk2023.epistemic_model: Socio-economic psychology of energy transition; regional political economy

zumofen2025.abstract: New technologies are necessary for energy system transition and meeting climate targets. However, obstacles to social acceptance, often linked to limited understanding and awareness, impede their integration. This article focuses on the acceptance of seasonal thermal energy storage technologies. This energy technology enables the storage of surplus heat in summer for heating in winter and the transfer of cold from winter to summer for cooling purposes. Combining theoretical insights from research on public opinion formation and social acceptance, this article constructs a model to explore how different information framings and formats influence individual opinion formation and the social acceptance of these technologies. It presents data from an experiment conducted in Switzerland through two online cross-sectional surveys (N = 1749; N = 614). The participants were given varied information framing conditions and formats. Based on independent sample t-tests, Kruskal-Wallis tests, and generalized structural equation models, the findings reveal that providing identical information in a video rather than as text increases general technology acceptance directly, as well as indirectly through reduced information complexity. Emphasizing technological readiness also positively affects general technology acceptance. However, these effects do not extend to more concrete market and community acceptance. The research highlights the significance of tailored and accessible information in facilitating information processing for unknown (energy) technologies in enhancing their social acceptance.
zumofen2025.title: The Influence of Information Format and Framing on Acceptance of Energy Storage Technologies
zumofen2025.author: Zumofen, Guillaume and Stadelmann-Steffen, Isabelle and Strater, Rebeka
zumofen2025.description: Experimental study examining how information framing and format influence social acceptance of seasonal thermal energy storage technologies in Switzerland.
zumofen2025.epistemic_model: Public opinion formation theory and social acceptance research
zumofen2025.method: Experimental design with two online cross-sectional surveys (N=1749, N=614)

campos2022a.researcherid-numbers: Conceição Firmino De Souza, Debora/KFB-9930-2024 Luz, Guilherme/ABH-2754-2021 Campos, Ines/AAK-5822-2021 Lima, Aias/JHT-5553-2023 Pera, David/P-3579-2015 Brito, Miguel/K-8476-2012
campos2022a.abstract: The purpose of the article is to contribute to structuring the problem of how to advance a sustainable energy transition and achieve carbon neutrality goals while ensuring a democratic and inclusive process, by drawing on a pilot case - i.e., the energy transition in Portugal. By building on approaches and concepts from the Sustainability Transitions research field, the article explores perceptions, values, and concerns regarding distributed and centralized energy models; inclusivity and energy democracy; energy systems' sustainability concerns and the speed of the transition. The study draws on the hypothesis that stakeholders across the state, market, community and third sector spheres, while equally supporting decarbonization, have different perceptions, values, and concerns regarding the social, environmental, and technological dynamics of the energy transition that need to be better understood for accelerating the transition. The multi-method approach included interviews, a survey (N = 110) and a stakeholder workshop, to unpack the key values and preferences around energy system technologies, sustainability and inclusionary aspects, the role of centralized and distributed energy systems and new investments, namely in green hydrogen and lithium mining. The results indicate there is a significant convergence on the fact that decarbonization is a priority that needs to be supported by inclusive and democratic processes. Decentralization, energy communities and solar energy are extremely valued, and transparency and information sharing are crucial expectations for new lithium mining projects, large-scale solar and green hydrogen investments. These findings outline some avenues for future research, where participation and transparency become anchors for a sustainable and inclusive transition.
campos2022a.title: Structuring the Problem of an Inclusive and Sustainable Energy Transition - A Pilot Study
campos2022a.author: Campos, Ines and Brito, Miguel and De Souza, Debora and Santino, Aias and Luz, Guilherme and Pera, David
campos2022a.description: Examines stakeholder perceptions, values, and concerns regarding energy transition models, inclusivity, and sustainability in Portugal's decarbonization process.

burke2018a.shorttitle: Political Power and Renewable Energy Futures
burke2018a.abstract: Inspired by the energy democracy movement, this conceptual review critically explores relationships between concentrated or distributed renewable energy and political power. Advocates assert that because the renewable energy transition is fundamentally a political struggle, efforts to shift from fossil fuels and decarbonize societies will not prove effective without confronting and destabilizing dominant systems of energy power. The objectives of this paper include: 1) theorizing and exploring the relationships between renewable energy and political power, 2) critically assessing tensions associated with an energy democracy agenda, and 3) drawing out the implications for democratizing renewable energy development in practice. Distributed energy-politics posits that distributed energy sources and technologies enable and organize distributed political power and vice versa. Efforts are underway to find ways to re-organize distributed energy flows into aggregated and concentrated stocks of energy and other forms of political power. More democratic renewable energy futures may benefit from strengthening democratic practices and outcomes, extending democratization of energy systems across all components, stages and end uses, and sharpening positions relative to dominant pressures of capitalism and market ideology, the ideology of unlimited growth, and the modernist/industrialist agenda. Renewable energy systems offer a possibility but not a certainty for more democratic energy futures.
burke2018a.title: Political Power and Renewable Energy Futures: {{A}} Critical Review
burke2018a.author: Burke, Matthew J. and Stephens, Jennie C.
burke2018a.description: Conceptual review exploring relationships between distributed/concentrated renewable energy systems and political power through energy democracy lens.
burke2018a.epistemic_model: Political ecology, energy democracy theory, critical political economy

melnyk2025.abstract: In this report, we present a framework for mapping the ethical dilemmas that arise in the development of offshore wind parks in the North Sea. The development of new technologies, such as offshore wind parks, gives rise to ethical dilemmas. These dilemmas can be characterised in terms of conflicts between relevant values, which we identified through a review of the literature on the ethics of technology and through consultation with stakeholders. With the input of stakeholders, these values have then been systematically categorised so they can be interpreted in terms of ethical dilemmas. Our analysis of the input from the stakeholder workshop reveals a deep concern for balancing the Dutch energy transition with the ecological preservation of the North Sea and its ecosystems. When identifying values, stakeholders noted that it is important that the energy transition is not considered in isolation from other pressures on the North Sea. This includes other significant energy-related developments, such as gas exploration and deep-sea mining in the North Sea. Stakeholders observed that the current EU regulations are not adequately addressing these cumulative pressures caused by wind farms, other activities in the North Sea, and the impact of climate change. Therefore, stakeholders believe that EU-level and Dutch-level regulations should reflect these complexities in a more ethically informed manner. Our reflections also highlight the need for adaptive policies and institutions that would better reflect the complexities of cumulative pressures on the North Sea in a more ethically informed manner, accounting for evolving knowledge and values; the moral responsibilities not only of the Netherlands but also of other countries impacting the North Sea; and the long-term sustainability of energy infrastructure development. At its core, the output of the stakeholder workshop is not limited to the exploration of offshore wind energy but expands to questioning how to ensure that the Dutch energy transition contributes to climate goals without disproportionately harming the North Sea or creating new, unforeseen environmental and societal challenges. In other words, based on our analysis of the insights from the workshop, we can confirm that the question is broader than environmental concerns regarding, for instance, bird mortality. The executed study shows the necessity of understanding the relations between spatial, temporal, and environmental challenges. From this perspective, ethical issues exceed an isolated focus on the ecological impacts of offshore wind energy to signify the importance of ethical scrutiny of cumulative and interrelated effects of Dutch energy transition development on the North Sea. Our recommendations expand on a proposed integrated values-oriented research agenda for the Dutch energy transition.
melnyk2025.title: Navigating the north sea dilemmas
melnyk2025.author: Melnyk, Anna; Taebi, Behnam; Gammon, Andrea; Hutton, James; Pesch, Udo

Acceptability.reasoning: Acceptability assigned to fiducial aspect [15] as it reflects value-based judgements and belief systems about energy systems. Primarily enables Policy and influences Citizenship Behavior, indicating a socio-political facilitator role. Co-occurs with Modeling in analytical contexts. Socio-political dimension [3] reflects its role in institutional legitimacy and governance. Moderate frequency (10) and sources (6) support MEDIUM confidence.
Acceptability.ontology_description: Acceptability represents the value-based judgement of whether energy systems and transitions are deemed legitimate, appropriate, or tolerable by stakeholders. It encompasses embedded values assessment, emotional responses to sustainable energy proposals, and judgements that shape citizenship behavior. Functions as a precondition for policy effectiveness and institutional legitimacy in energy governance contexts.

Acceptability_Stability.reasoning: Aspect 6: Sensitive—captures perceptual consistency and emotional stability in judgments. Relations show influences on acceptance stability via ambivalence and novelty. Co-factors (Technology Novelty, Ambivalence) clarify psychological context. Dimension 1: Community/individual-level acceptance dynamics. Low frequency (3) and single source limit confidence.
Acceptability_Stability.ontology_description: The temporal consistency and reliability of individuals' acceptability judgments toward energy technologies. Stability varies with technology novelty, personal importance, and ambivalence—novel technologies elicit less stable judgments than established ones. Reflects the robustness of psychological attitudes over time, influencing predictability of public acceptance patterns.

Acceptance.reasoning: Social aspect (10) captures community relations and collective dynamics. Primarily enables Energy Transition and constrains Deployment. Co-occurs with Policy, Participation, Wind Energy. Community acceptance dimension (1) reflects local stakeholder relevance. High frequency (414) and broad sources (179) indicate central concept.
Acceptance.ontology_description: Social acceptance represents the degree to which communities, stakeholders, and citizens approve of and support energy transition technologies and projects. It encompasses public attitudes, local consent, and collective willingness to host or adopt renewable energy systems. Critical determinant of project deployment success, influenced by participation, design choices, and perceived benefits. Distinguished from market or policy acceptance by its focus on community-level social dynamics.

Acceptance_Assessment.reasoning: Analytical aspect (7) as methodological evaluation framework. Enables understanding through survey/social media analysis. Co-factors: Survey, Social Media Data clarify research tools. Technical-scientific dimension (4) reflects systematic assessment approach. Low frequency (2) and single source limit robustness.
Acceptance_Assessment.ontology_description: Methodological framework for evaluating public acceptance and awareness of energy technologies through systematic data collection and analysis. Combines survey instruments and social media datasets to measure stakeholder perceptions. Research approach that quantifies acceptance levels and identifies awareness patterns in energy transition contexts.

Acceptance_Criteria.reasoning: Aspect 13 (juridical): organizational standards and requirements for technology adoption. Relation profile: enables Implementation (functional facilitator). Co-occurs with Implementation in corporate governance context. Dimension 3: institutional decision-making frameworks. Low frequency/sources limit robustness.
Acceptance_Criteria.ontology_description: Organizational or institutional standards and requirements that companies apply when evaluating and approving energy transition technologies for implementation. These criteria function as decision-making frameworks that determine whether innovations meet organizational, regulatory, or performance thresholds necessary for adoption and deployment in corporate settings.

Acceptance_Dimension.reasoning: Social aspect (10) as it refers to layered structures of community-level social acceptance. Influences acceptance, suggesting dimensional framework role. Co-occurs with Acceptance, clarifying community vs socio-political levels. Community dimension (1) via local stakeholder focus. Low frequency/single source limits confidence.
Acceptance_Dimension.ontology_description: Conceptual framework distinguishing multiple layers of social acceptance in energy transitions, particularly differentiating community-level acceptance from socio-political acceptance. Represents the structural categorization of acceptance phenomena across different stakeholder groups and governance scales, acknowledging technology-specific and experience-dependent variation in acceptance patterns.

Acceptance_Sensitivity.reasoning: Sensitive aspect (6): Perceptual-psychological construct measuring responsiveness to acceptance stimuli. Influences psychological distance and familiarity. Co-occurs with political support and familiarity. Community dimension: local stakeholder perception. Low frequency/sources indicate tentative classification.
Acceptance_Sensitivity.ontology_description: Psychological construct reflecting individual or group responsiveness and susceptibility to acceptance-related stimuli in energy transition contexts. Represents the degree to which actors' acceptance attitudes are malleable or influenced by psychological distance, familiarity with technology, and political support levels. Context-dependent sensitivity varying across populations with different exposure to specific technologies like CCS.

Access.reasoning: Aspect 13 (Juridical): Access relates to governance frameworks enabling technology/service availability. Relations show enabling role (Transition) and analytical relevance (Modeling). Co-occurs with planning/technology contexts. Dimension 3: Socio-political—concerns institutional mechanisms for equitable access. Moderate frequency (4) and sources (3) indicate emerging concept.
Access.ontology_description: Access denotes the institutional and procedural conditions enabling equitable availability of energy technologies and services. In energy transition contexts, it encompasses both physical availability (e.g., PAYG LPG for clean cooking) and procedural dimensions (transparency in planning processes). Access functions as a governance mechanism determining who can benefit from energy transitions, bridging technological deployment with social equity considerations.

Accessibility.reasoning: Accessibility is spatial (aspect 2) as it concerns physical location and geographic relation to distribution systems and communities. Relations show it influences Acceptance and Site Selection. Co-factors include Site Selection and community-relevant Methodology, indicating local stakeholder context. Community acceptance dimension (1) fits tribal research and social requirements context. Moderate frequency (3) and sources (3) suggest emerging importance.
Accessibility.ontology_description: Accessibility denotes the spatial and logistical ease of reaching energy infrastructure sites, including hydrogen storage facilities and renewable energy installations. It encompasses geographic proximity to distribution networks, physical access for construction and maintenance, and community-centered accessibility for culturally relevant engagement. In site selection processes, accessibility balances technical requirements with social inclusion, ensuring infrastructure can be physically integrated into existing systems while remaining reachable for diverse stakeholder groups.

Accuracy.reasoning: Aspect [7]: Analytical—relates to research methodology and technical assessment quality. Mainly enables Decision Making. Co-occurs with methodological evaluation. Dimension [4]: Technical-scientific—concerns scientific method quality in visualisation studies. Low frequency (1) and single source indicate limited evidence.
Accuracy.ontology_description: The precision and technical quality of visual impact assessment methodologies, particularly in wind farm visualisation studies. Refers to the degree to which imaging techniques and representation methods faithfully depict the visual appearance of proposed energy infrastructure, supporting reliable spatial planning and stakeholder communication. Critical for maintaining credibility of assessment processes.

Action.reasoning: Kinematic (3): Action represents behavioral movement toward energy transition participation. Relations show connection to Awareness-Readiness chain, suggesting action as outcome of psychological readiness. Co-factors (Awareness, Readiness) indicate progression from cognition to behavior. Community dimension (1): Context reflects citizen-level investment decisions in local energy systems. Low frequency (1) and single source limit generalizability.
Action.ontology_description: Action represents the behavioral manifestation of citizen engagement in energy transition, specifically the willingness to take concrete investment steps in renewable energy technologies and smart appliances. It reflects the conversion of awareness and readiness into tangible participation behaviors. In acceptance research, action signifies the critical transition from passive support to active involvement, distinguishing intention from implementation at the household or community level.

Action_Situation.reasoning: Aspect 8 (Formative): represents planning/design contexts that shape social dynamics. Relations show influences on Acceptance. Co-occurs with Opinion, Acceptance—situational framing context. Dimension 1: community-level opinion crystallization. Low frequency (1) and single source limit robustness.
Action_Situation.ontology_description: Conceptual framing derived from institutional analysis theory representing the structured context in which community opinions about energy projects form and crystallize. Describes the situational arena where diffuse, heterogeneous community attitudes coalesce into collective positions regarding social license to operate. Functions as the decision-making environment that mediates between individual opinions and collective acceptance outcomes in local energy transition contexts.

Activity_Interference.reasoning: Aspect 8 (Formative): Factor concerns planning and design conflicts in marine spatial contexts. Relation: constrains implementation processes. Co-occurrence: Implementation clarifies operational scope. Dimension 1: Local stakeholder conflicts in marine area planning. Low frequency (1) and single source limit robustness.
Activity_Interference.ontology_description: Represents conflicts between different marine spatial uses (energy infrastructure, fishing, tourism, navigation) that complicate integrated planning. Arises when multiple economic, recreational, or conservation activities compete for shared marine space, requiring coordinated design and inclusive planning practices to resolve overlapping claims and operational incompatibilities in offshore energy development.

Actor.reasoning: Aspect 10: Social nature reflects stakeholder roles and agency in energy transition. Relations show actors influence policy deployment and participation. Co-occurs with governance and deployment factors. Dimension 3: Socio-political context—utilities, grid operators, project initiators shape institutional outcomes. Medium confidence: frequency 3, sources 3.
Actor.ontology_description: Refers to stakeholders and organizational entities involved in energy transition processes, including energy utilities, grid operators, project initiators, and carbon-intensive regional actors. Encompasses individuals and organizations that make strategic decisions, test technologies, implement projects, and influence policy outcomes. Their agency, choices, and initiatives determine deployment pathways, participation structures, and governance approaches in local and systemic energy transitions.

Actor_Relationship.reasoning: Aspect 10: Social domain—focuses on relational dynamics between collective energy actors. Relation type: enables formation of prosumer collectives and alters energy system interactions. Co-factors: prosumer collectives, storage modes—indicating community-level configurations. Dimension 1: community acceptance context with local stakeholder networks. Low frequency (n=1) limits robustness.
Actor_Relationship.ontology_description: Refers to the evolving interpersonal and inter-organizational connections among energy system participants, particularly in the context of prosumer collectives and distributed energy storage. Encompasses shifting roles, dependencies, and collaboration patterns as households, utilities, and grid operators reconfigure their relationships through new socio-technical arrangements. Central to understanding how decentralized energy models transform traditional utility-consumer dynamics into multi-actor coordination networks within community energy systems.

Adaptive_Management.reasoning: Aspect 8 (formative): planning approach enabling iterative decision-making and model refinement. Enables consensus through flexible design processes. Co-occurs with decision-making and uncertainty documentation. Socio-political dimension: institutional decision-making context. Low frequency limits robustness.
Adaptive_Management.ontology_description: A formative governance approach enabling iterative refinement of decisions and models over extended periods. Involves retaining observational databases, assigning confidence levels to models, and treating outcomes as evolving rather than final. Facilitates consensus-building through flexible adjustment to new information and stakeholder input in long-term energy transition planning processes.

Administrative_Complexity.reasoning: Juridical aspect: procedural and regulatory burden in governance systems. Primarily constrains Harmonization, indicating regulatory friction. Co-occurs with Harmonization in multi-level governance context. Socio-political dimension: institutional coordination challenge. Low frequency (1) and single source limit confidence.
Administrative_Complexity.ontology_description: Administrative complexity refers to the procedural burden and regulatory intricacy associated with implementing policy harmonization in energy transition governance. It encompasses duplicated processes, complicated administrative requirements, and contradictory regulatory frameworks that create friction in multi-level governance coordination. Stakeholders perceive it as a trade-off risk against the benefits of standardized certification and labeling systems.

Administrative_Obstacle.reasoning: Aspect 13: Juridical—administrative/regulatory barrier in implementation process. Constrains renewable implementation. Co-occurs with economic/technological barriers. Dimension 3: Socio-political—institutional governance context affecting policy execution. Low frequency (n=1) indicates tentative classification.
Administrative_Obstacle.ontology_description: Administrative obstacles refer to bureaucratic, procedural, or institutional barriers within governance systems that impede the implementation of renewable energy technologies. These obstacles include regulatory hurdles, permitting delays, coordination failures across agencies, and institutional inefficiencies that constrain energy transition progress alongside economic and technological factors.

Adoption.reasoning: Formative aspect: involves planning and implementation of innovations. Primarily enables Technology, Market, and Planning. Co-occurs with policy, technology, and acceptance factors. Market dimension: focuses on consumer/investor uptake patterns. High frequency (65) and broad sources (22) confirm centrality.

Encompasses implementation decisions by governments, businesses, and households. Influenced by policy frameworks, financial feasibility, social acceptance, and user attitudes.
